steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle has four stages: (1) Plan (hypothesis and strategy), (2) Collect (obtain data), (3) Process (calculate and represent), (4) Interpret (analyse and conclude)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Exam questions often ask you to identify which stage a given task belongs to or to describe what happens at each stage

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Planning includes: writing a clear hypothesis, identifying the population, choosing a sampling method, deciding what data to collect and how to collect it

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Data collection includes: designing data collection sheets, pilot studies, dealing with non-response, and ensuring data is reliable and unbiased

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: A student wants to investigate whether Year 11 students spend more time on homework than Year 8 students. State a suitable hypothesis and identify the population. | Q: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using a pilot study. | Q: A survey on exercise habits was conducted by posting questionnaires to 500 households. Only 120 were returned. Identify two sources of bias and explain how each affects the results.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When a question names a stage of the SEC, give specific detail about what happens — do not just repeat the stage name Always link conclusions back to the original hypothesis using specific data values from the question In evaluation questions, give at least two points: one strength and one weakness, each explained with reasoning When asked to design an investigation, structure your answer using the four SEC stages to ensure completeness Marks for SEC questions often come from ‘justification’ — always explain why a method is chosen, not just what it is
